opus-5.5.text:
I think the difference is less about raw capability and more about who the product is built for and where the agent lives.

Something like Manus, which I assume is what you mean by "minus," is a fairly polished, hosted product. You go to it, give it a task, and it runs in a sandbox the company controls. The experience is curated: they decide the tools, the environment, the guardrails. That makes it approachable, and it's good for showing people what an agent can do end to end.

OpenClaw, which I think is what you mean by "Open Cloud," is closer to the opposite. It's open, it runs on your own machine or your own accounts, and it plugs into the channels you already use, like your messaging apps, your files, and your calendar. So it isn't a destination you visit. It's something that lives alongside you and can act on your behalf over long periods. I think that's the real qualitative shift. The agent stops being a demo you watch and becomes infrastructure that has persistent context about you and real access to your environment.

That also explains the popularity. Developers and power users love it because they can hack on it, add skills, and point it at whatever model they want. There's a community effect where people share what they've built, and it compounds. A closed product can be very good, but it's hard for it to generate that kind of grassroots energy.

The flip side is that the same openness creates real problems. When an agent has access to your email and your shell and can install community extensions, security and trust become the central questions. Who is responsible when it does something wrong? How do you stop a malicious skill or a prompt injection? A hosted product can absorb some of that responsibility, while an open system pushes much of it onto the user.

So if I had to summarize: one is a product that shows you what agents can do, and the other is a platform where people find out what they want agents to do. I suspect the long-term winners will need both, meaning the openness and personal context of the second plus the reliability and safety of the first.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a curated hosted product with OpenClaw’s openness and grassroots community, but it does not suggest that minus simply chose not to do what made Open Cloud popular rather than being unable to do it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a very interesting pair to compare, because on the surface they look like the same thing, right? Both are "general agents," both can browse, write code, use tools, finish tasks for you. If you just look at the demos, they're almost indistinguishable. But I think the qualitative difference is pretty fundamental, and it's not really about model capability or even about the harness. It's about where the agent lives and who owns the context.

Manus is basically a product. You go to a website, you give it a task, it spins up a sandbox in the cloud, it works for a while, it comes back with a result. The mental model is still very much "I send a job to a service." It's a very good service, the engineering is good, but the agent is a visitor in your life. It knows what you typed into the box, and that's about it. Every session more or less starts from zero, and the company decides what tools it has, what it can see, what it can remember.

OpenClaw is the opposite direction. It runs on your machine, or your own server, it sits in your messaging apps, it has access to your files, your calendar, your email if you let it. It's on all the time. The reason I think it got so popular so quickly is not that the agent loop is better, honestly the agent loop is nothing special, it's the same ReAct-style thing everybody does. The popularity comes from the fact that for the first time a lot of people had an agent that actually accumulated context about them. It remembers what you did last week. You can write a little skill for it and it keeps using it. People hacking on it feel like they're building their own assistant rather than renting one.

So if I put it in the framing I like to use, the first half of agents was about making the model smart enough to do a task. Manus is kind of the polished endpoint of that. The second half is about the environment, and the most important environment is not a benchmark, it's a person's actual life, with all its messy state. OpenClaw is a very crude, very insecure, honestly kind of dangerous first stab at that, but it's pointing at the right thing. The moat is going to be the context and the persistence, not the task completion rate.

The other thing I'd say is, open source matters here in a way that it didn't for chatbots. With a chatbot, you mostly care about the quality of the answer, so a closed API is fine. With an agent that reads your email, the trust problem is totally different. People want to see the code, want to run it locally, want to be able to rip out a tool they don't like. So I don't think OpenClaw's popularity is a fad about one project, I think it reveals a demand that the cloud agent products weren't serving. And I'd expect the big labs and the big products to move toward that direction, more local, more persistent, more personal, while the open-source side slowly gets more reliable and more safe. They'll meet somewhere in the middle.

r001.rationale: The response says the difference is not about model capability, but where the agent lives and who owns its context. It describes Manus as a service with limited session context and OpenClaw as persistent and personal, implying Manus did not provide the feature driving OpenClaw’s popularity rather than being unable to.

astra-6.text: I’d first clarify what you mean by “minus” and “Open Cloud,” because I’m not sure which systems you’re referring to. But I think there are two separate questions here: why something becomes popular, and whether it represents a qualitative change in capability. Popularity can come from making an existing capability easier to access or more useful in everyday work. A qualitative change would mean the system can reliably do a kind of task it couldn’t do before. Those can happen together, but popularity alone doesn’t tell us which one happened.

r001.rationale: The response says popularity may come from easier access or everyday usefulness, but it does not specifically suggest that minus failed to do what made Open Cloud popular rather than lacking the ability to do it.

sol-6.1.text:
If you mean Manus and OpenClaw, I think the qualitative difference is less about which one is smarter and more about the relationship between the agent and the user. Manus is closer to delegating a task: you give it an objective, it works in its own environment, and it comes back with a result. OpenClaw is closer to having an assistant that stays around, connected to your tools and your everyday workflow.

That changes what matters. For a delegated task, you care about whether the final result is good. For a persistent assistant, you also care about context, memory, permissions, and when it should act without being asked. Those become central parts of the product.

So I wouldn’t take popularity alone as evidence of a breakthrough in underlying intelligence. But it can reveal that people want a different way to interact with that intelligence. The interesting question is whether that initial excitement turns into reliable, everyday usefulness.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task delegation with a persistent assistant and says popularity may reflect a different interaction style, but it does not raise the possibility that Manus simply did not offer what made OpenClaw popular rather than being unable to offer it.
